issues.current_content:
Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pipelines consist of multiple distinct steps, each of which should be individually traced. A typical RAG trace hierarchy begins with a root span for the entire query, then nests child spans for each processing stage.

The embedding step converts the user query into a vector. Its span should record the embedding model name, input token count, and latency. The retrieval step queries a vector store; its span should capture the number of candidates requested (top-k), the number of results returned, each document's ID and similarity score, and the vector database provider.

When a reranker is applied, a dedicated child span records the reranking model name, the input document count, and the output document count after filtering by a score threshold. Recording before-and-after score distributions allows teams to evaluate whether reranking improves context quality.

Using OpenTelemetry, each stage is represented as a child span under a common parent. Span links or baggage can propagate the original query context across all child spans, enabling full-pipeline analysis in tools like Jaeger, Grafana Tempo, or LangSmith.

title.en: Difference between MLOps, LLMOps and app observability

body.en: In this lesson you will learn: 1) How MLOps, LLMOps, and application observability differ and where they overlap 2) What to monitor across data, models, prompts, and services 3) How to choose controls, telemetry, and workflows to improve reliability, quality, and cost

blocks.title: Prompt Versioning Explained | The Missing Piece of Production LLMOps
blocks.label: Course Video

objectiveBefore.fr: Pendant cette vidéo, repérez les éléments qui illustrent « What You Will Learn » avant de poursuivre.
objectiveBefore.en: While watching, identify the elements that illustrate “What You Will Learn” before continuing.

body.en:
MLOps focuses on the lifecycle of traditional ML models: data management, training pipelines, validation, model registry, deployment, and drift/quality monitoring. Typical practices include CI/CD/CT for data and models, feature stores, reproducible training, canary/blue-green deployments, and monitoring data drift, concept drift, and serving parity.

LLMOps extends MLOps to generative AI systems. It adds prompt and template management, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipelines, tool/function calling, guardrails and safety checks, evaluation of faithfulness and toxicity, prompt/model/version lineage, prompt/inference caching, cost/latency/token monitoring, and human/AI feedback loops. Because LLM outputs are stochastic and context-dependent, LLMOps emphasizes scenario-based eval sets, automatic metrics (e.g., groundedness), human review, and continuous prompt/retrieval/model iteration.

Application observability instruments the running system for reliability and performance: logs, metrics, and traces (often via OpenTelemetry), RED/USE methods, SLOs/SLIs, error budgets, and distributed tracing across services. It answers "what is happening" in production and where latency/errors occur in the request path.

How they interact: observability shows symptoms (e.g., p95 latency, errors), while MLOps/LLMOps target ML-specific causes (data drift, prompt regressions, hallucinations). For LLM apps, combine service-level telemetry (requests, traces, saturation) with ML/LLM signals (prompt versions, retrieval quality, token counts, safety flags, eval scores). Governance spans all three: lineage, approvals, privacy/security, and auditability.

• MLOps vs LLMOps: MLOps centers on datasets, features, training, and classic inference; LLMOps adds prompts, retrieval/tooling, generative evals, and safety/guardrails.
• App observability: System-wide telemetry (logs/metrics/traces) for reliability, latency, and SLOs; complementary to but distinct from ML/LLM quality monitoring.
• Unified telemetry: Correlate trace IDs with model/prompt versions, token counts, RAG scores, and eval results to debug quality, cost, and latency end to end.

• MLOps manages data/model lifecycles; LLMOps adds prompt, retrieval, tools, and generative evals/safety.
• Application observability reveals runtime behavior (latency, errors, traces) across services.
• Combine system telemetry with ML/LLM signals to diagnose quality, reliability, and cost holistically.
Congratulations! You have completed this lesson. You can now distinguish MLOps, LLMOps, and app observability and know how to instrument and monitor LLM systems end to end.

title.en: AI lifecycle: prompt, retrieval, tools, model, output, feedback

body.en: In this lesson you will learn: 1) The end-to-end LLM application lifecycle from prompt to feedback 2) Key design choices, telemetry, and risks at each stage 3) How to iterate using evaluations and feedback to improve quality, latency, and cost

Prompt: Define roles, instructions, and templates with variables; manage versions and test sets; enforce guardrails (e.g., system prompts, policies). Capture prompt IDs in traces for reproducibility.

Retrieval: RAG fetches context from knowledge sources. Ingest, chunk, embed, and index documents; use vector/hybrid search and query rewriting. Monitor recall@k, MRR, and staleness; refresh embeddings and indexes as content changes.

Tools: Enable function calling for external actions (search, DB, calculators). Define strict tool schemas, timeouts, retries, and fallbacks; log tool selection and errors. Restrict capabilities with least privilege and input/output validation.

Model: Choose model family/provider, context window, and parameters (temperature, top_p). Monitor token usage, latency, and cost; cache frequent prompts/responses; consider smaller or specialized models for cost/latency wins.

Output: Post-process and validate responses. Use JSON mode/structured output, schema validators, and safety filters (toxicity/PII). Apply hallucination checks and groundedness/faithfulness metrics on sampled traffic.

Feedback: Collect explicit ratings and implicit signals (clicks, task success). Store with lineage (prompt/retrieval/model versions). Use offline evals, canary/A/B tests, and feedback-driven updates (e.g., add to eval sets, adjust prompts, retrain retriever, or fine-tune). Close the loop with dashboards and alerting on quality SLOs.

title.en: Quality, latency, cost and safety as SLO dimensions

body.en: In this lesson you will learn: 1) How to define Quality, Latency, Cost, and Safety (QLCS) as measurable SLIs and set SLO targets. 2) How to use error budgets and burn-rate alerting to operate LLM systems. 3) How to manage trade-offs (e.g., model choice, temperature, caching, routing, guardrails) to meet SLOs.

SLOs (Service Level Objectives) are target levels for user-facing performance; SLIs (Service Level Indicators) are the measurements; SLAs are contractual commitments. In LLMOps, four core SLO dimensions matter:

Quality: How well the system achieves task goals. Common SLIs include exact match/accuracy (for structured Q&A), BLEU/ROUGE for summarization (with caution), factuality/hallucination rate, relevance score for RAG, toxicity/harassment rate, user satisfaction (CSAT/Thumbs-up), and intervention/escalation rate. Use offline eval suites (gold datasets, unit tests) and online signals (A/B tests, implicit feedback). Calibrate with human review for safety-critical tasks.

Latency: How quickly users receive useful output. SLIs include time-to-first-token (TTFT), time-to-last-token (TTLT), end-to-end latency, and tail latency (p95/p99). Track by request class (e.g., cold vs. warm cache), and consider queue time, retrieval time, model compute time, and post-processing.

Cost: Resources consumed per outcome. SLIs include tokens per request, cost per 1k tokens (input/output), cost per successful task, GPU-seconds per request, or monthly cost per active user. Track cache hit rate, prompt length, and model/router mix. Define SLOs as budget ceilings (e.g., ≤ $0.01 per request p95; ≤ $X/day).

Safety: Risk of harmful or policy-violating outputs. SLIs include policy-violation rate, unsafe content rate, jailbreak success rate, PII redaction failure rate, and moderation false-negative rate. Use layered defenses: prompt hardening, safety classifiers, allow/deny lists, and human-in-the-loop.

Trade-offs: Increasing context or using larger models often improves quality but increases latency and cost; aggressive safety filters may add latency or reduce recall. Techniques to balance include: caching (prompt/embedding), streaming responses (improve perceived latency), response truncation/early cutoff, adaptive routing (easy vs. hard queries), temperature/top-p tuning, reranking smaller candidates before large-model calls, and selective safety checks.

Error budgets and alerting: An SLO of 99% success implies 1% error budget. Use multi-window, multi-burn-rate alerts (e.g., 14.4× over 5 min; 2× over 1 h) for fast detection and stability. Align SLO windows with user expectations (e.g., weekly for consumer chat, daily for enterprise).

• SLIs vs SLOs vs SLAs: What you measure, what you target, what you promise.
• Error budgets and burn-rate alerts: Quantify allowable failure and detect rapid budget consumption.
• Q–L–C–S trade-offs: Techniques (caching, routing, streaming, guardrails) to optimize one dimension without breaking others.

• Define clear SLIs for Quality, Latency, Cost, and Safety and set realistic SLO targets.
• Use error budgets and burn-rate alerts to operate proactively.
• Balance Q–L–C–S with tactics like caching, streaming, routing, and guardrails.
Congratulations! You have completed this lesson. You now understand the core concepts and can apply them in practice.

title.en: Logs vs traces vs metrics for AI applications

body.en: In this lesson you will learn: 1) The purpose and differences between logs, traces, and metrics in AI/LLM systems. 2) How to instrument LLM pipelines (retrieval, prompting, generation, safety) with OpenTelemetry-style signals. 3) How to use each signal for debugging, SLOs, and governance while controlling cost and privacy.

Logs: Immutable, timestamped records of events with rich, often high-cardinality context. For LLM apps, prefer structured logs (JSON) containing request_id, user/session (pseudonymized), prompt ID/template version, input hash, retrieved document IDs/snippets, model name/params (temperature, top_p), token counts, moderation results, cost estimates, and output summary or full text (with redaction). Use log levels, sampling, PII scrubbing, and retention policies to control privacy and storage cost.

Traces: Causal view of a single request across services. A trace contains spans (e.g., HTTP ingress → embed → vector search → rerank → prompt build → model call → safety check → post-processing). Each span has start/end timestamps, attributes (e.g., index_name, k, model, prompt_tokens), events (e.g., retry, timeout), and status. Propagate context using W3C Trace Context (trace_id, span_id). Traces pinpoint where latency or errors occur and link to logs via IDs; exemplars can link metrics to representative traces.

Metrics: Aggregated, numeric time series for SLOs and alerting. Types: counters (tokens_consumed_total, requests_total, violations_total), gauges (queue_depth), and histograms (latency_ms, prompt_length_tokens). Compute p50/p95, error rate, cost per minute, cache hit ratio. Keep label cardinality under control (e.g., limit to model_name, route, tenant) to avoid excessive series.

Choosing signals: Use metrics for SLOs/alerts and capacity planning; traces to localize issues and analyze tail latency; logs to debug content correctness, safety incidents, and audits. Combine them: alert (metric) → jump to exemplar trace → inspect related logs for prompts/docs/outputs.

Governance and cost: Redact PII in logs, use content hashing, separate sensitive payload storage, and apply retention windows. Sample verbose logs, keep full traces for problem segments, and downsample low-value metrics. Document schemas to ensure consistency across components.

• Structured logs capture rich context (prompts, retrieved docs, outputs) for debugging and audits.
• Distributed traces connect components end-to-end with spans, timings, and errors to localize issues.
• Metrics provide aggregated SLIs/SLOs (latency, error, cost) and power alerting; manage label cardinality.

• Use metrics for SLOs and alerting, traces to localize issues, and logs to debug content and safety.
• Propagate trace context and align schemas so signals can be correlated.
• Control privacy and cost with redaction, sampling, and label cardinality limits.
Congratulations! You have completed this lesson. You now understand the core concepts and can apply them in practice.

title.en: Tracing Model Calls: Provider, Model, Tokens and Latency

body.en:
Tracing LLM model calls is the foundation of AI observability. Every call to a model provider such as OpenAI, Anthropic, or a self-hosted endpoint should be wrapped in a trace span that captures key metadata.

A well-structured model call span includes the provider name (e.g., openai), the specific model identifier (e.g., gpt-4o), and token counts broken down into prompt tokens, completion tokens, and totals. These attributes allow you to correlate cost, performance, and quality over time.

Latency is measured as the wall-clock time from request initiation to the first byte of the response (time-to-first-token, TTFT) and the total response time. Capturing both gives insight into streaming behavior versus batch responses.

Using OpenTelemetry, spans are created with start and end timestamps automatically. Custom attributes such as llm.provider, llm.model, llm.usage.prompt_tokens, llm.usage.completion_tokens, and llm.latency_ms are added via the span.set_attribute() API, enabling downstream querying and alerting in your observability backend.

title.en: Tracing RAG Retrieval and Reranking Steps

body.en:
Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pipelines consist of multiple distinct steps, each of which should be individually traced. A typical RAG trace hierarchy begins with a root span for the entire query, then nests child spans for each processing stage.

The embedding step converts the user query into a vector. Its span should record the embedding model name, input token count, and latency. The retrieval step queries a vector store; its span should capture the number of candidates requested (top-k), the number of results returned, each document's ID and similarity score, and the vector database provider.

When a reranker is applied, a dedicated child span records the reranking model name, the input document count, and the output document count after filtering by a score threshold. Recording before-and-after score distributions allows teams to evaluate whether reranking improves context quality.

Using OpenTelemetry, each stage is represented as a child span under a common parent. Span links or baggage can propagate the original query context across all child spans, enabling full-pipeline analysis in tools like Jaeger, Grafana Tempo, or LangSmith.

title.en: Tracing Tool Calls and Agent Loops

body.en:
Agentic AI systems execute dynamic, multi-step workflows in which an LLM decides which tools to call, evaluates results, and may loop multiple times before producing a final answer. Tracing these systems requires capturing both the agent's reasoning cycle and each discrete tool invocation.

The agent loop itself is represented as a root or parent span. Each iteration of the loop adds a child span that records the loop index, the LLM's chosen action, and the stop condition evaluation. Within each iteration, tool calls are modeled as grandchild spans. A tool call span should record the tool name, the serialized input arguments (with PII redacted), the output payload, and whether the call succeeded or raised an error.

Special attention is needed for recursive or parallel tool calls. In recursive cases, span depth increases with each nested call; depth limits should be monitored as a safety signal. In parallel execution, spans share the same parent but have overlapping time windows, which observability tools can visualize as concurrent branches.

Attributes such as agent.loop_iteration, agent.tool_name, agent.tool_status, and agent.final_answer_reached provide operators with the data needed to debug stuck loops, measure per-tool latency, and calculate the average number of reasoning steps required to complete a task.

question.en: In an agent trace, what is the correct span relationship between the agent loop and an individual tool call?

text.en: The tool call is a sibling span of the agent loop
The tool call is a child span of the agent loop span
The tool call creates a new root trace independent of the agent loop
The tool call span replaces the agent loop span

AI traces capture rich contextual data that is critical for debugging and monitoring, but they can also inadvertently contain sensitive information. User prompts may include names, email addresses, financial data, health records, or authentication tokens. Without redaction, this data flows into observability backends, violating privacy regulations and creating security risks.

Redaction must be applied at the span level before data leaves the application process. OpenTelemetry supports SpanProcessors that intercept every span before export. A custom SpanProcessor can inspect attribute values, apply regex patterns to detect PII (e.g., SSN, credit card numbers, email addresses), and replace matched content with a redaction token such as [REDACTED] or a pseudonymous hash.

For LLM prompt and response bodies, field-level masking can target specific JSON paths or named entity recognition (NER) can detect and redact entities dynamically. Tokenization replaces sensitive values with non-reversible identifiers that preserve referential consistency without exposing raw data.

Compliance frameworks impose specific requirements: GDPR mandates the right to erasure, meaning traces must not store personal data longer than necessary and must support deletion. HIPAA requires that PHI be de-identified before storage. SOC 2 requires audit trails of who accessed trace data. Implementing a trace data retention policy alongside redaction ensures holistic compliance.

In a SpanProcessor within the application process before export
In the OTEL Collector after it receives the spans

body.en:
Offline evaluation uses static datasets, labeled rubrics, and automated metrics to compare prompts/models safely before deployment. Typical metrics include task accuracy/EM, F1 for extraction, ROUGE/BLEU/BERTScore for summarization, toxicity and bias scores for safety, hallucination/factuality checks (e.g., retrieval-grounded correctness), as well as latency and cost. Techniques include golden sets, pairwise preference judgments, Elo/Bradley–Terry ranking, stratified data slicing, bootstrap confidence intervals, and cross-validation. Control leakage by keeping train/eval splits clean, deduplicating near-duplicates, and mirroring real traffic distribution.

Online evaluation measures impact on real users and systems. Use canary or A/B tests (or bandits) with clear primary KPIs (e.g., task success, deflection rate, CSAT), guardrail metrics (safety incidents, latency SLOs, error rate), and budgets (cost per 1k tokens). Ensure randomization, eligibility rules, and exposure controls. Apply power analysis for sample size, sequential testing to detect early wins or stop for harm, and segment results by slices (locale, task type) to catch regressions. Monitor drift and feedback loops; combine explicit ratings with implicit signals (click-through, resolution, rephrases). Connect offline and online by using offline gates to shortlist candidates, then validate causal impact online and update offline suites based on online learnings.

• Offline evaluation: fixed datasets, human rubrics, and automated metrics to de-risk changes before deployment
• Online evaluation: randomized experiments on real traffic to measure KPIs, safety, latency, and cost
• Slicing and significance: analyze by critical cohorts and use confidence intervals/p-values or sequential tests to avoid false wins

• Use offline evaluation to shortlist safe, promising candidates quickly
• Validate causal impact online with A/B or bandits, enforcing safety and latency guardrails
• Maintain cohort slicing and statistical rigor to avoid false signals and detect regressions

Treat prompts as first-class, immutable artifacts. Store full template text (system, user, tool instructions), variable names/defaults, and formatting constraints. Version all runtime parameters (temperature, top_p, max_tokens, stop, penalties), the exact model ID and revision, tokenizer, safety filters, and tool or function schemas. Track dependencies: RAG retriever/index versions, knowledge snapshots, guardrail policies, and evaluation datasets. Create an artifact manifest with a content hash and semver tag, and keep lineage links from dataset → prompt → model → release → evaluation results.

Experiment tracking should log inputs (redacted), rendered prompts, parameters, model/version, outputs, tokens, latency, cost, and user feedback. Protect privacy by redacting or hashing identifiers and enforcing access controls. Use CI/CD for prompts: propose changes via review, run offline gates, compare against baselines, then canary or A/B with rollback and change logs. Keep a changelog with semantic diffs of prompts, not just file diffs, to catch meaning-altering edits. Ensure reproducibility by pinning all versions and capturing environment metadata (SDK, provider, region, feature flags).

**In this lesson you will learn:**

Quality monitoring depends on systematic feedback loops. Explicit feedback includes user ratings (thumbs up/down), reason codes, and short comments; implicit feedback is derived from behavior such as message edits, abandonment, re-prompts, or downstream task success.

A good schema captures context (prompt, system state, retrieved docs), response, user segment, reason codes, and timestamps while respecting privacy (avoid storing raw PII, apply hashing/redaction). Sampling strategies combine stratified sampling across intents/risk tiers with active sampling of outliers (low confidence, drift signals) to maximize learning value. Feedback is triaged into: bug reports (prompt/policy fix), supervision data (fine-tuning/RLHF), and evaluation items (golden sets) to close the loop.

Regression gates enforce quality bars before deployment by comparing a candidate model or prompt to a frozen baseline on golden datasets and realistic replay logs. Gates should be multi-metric: task quality (exact match/F1, model-graded utility), safety (toxicity, PII leakage, hallucination), latency, and cost.

Because LLMs are stochastic, evaluate with multiple seeds or n-samples per prompt and summarize with means and confidence/credible intervals; require superiority on primary KPIs and non-inferiority (within a guardband) on safety/critical segments. Segment-level gates (e.g., payments, healthcare) prevent masking degradations by global averages.

Define pass/fail criteria and allowed deltas up front, and set minimum sample sizes to ensure power. Integrate these checks in CI/CD: automatic eval on PR, fail the build on gate violations, and require approvals for overrides.

After passing offline gates, use shadow testing and small canaries with real traffic, monitoring for drift, error budgets, and rollback triggers.

• Guardbands and non-inferiority: Predefined thresholds that prevent regressions on critical metrics and segments

title.en: Token Cost Spikes and Latency Incidents

body.en:
Token cost spikes occur when prompt length, output verbosity, or request volume suddenly increases beyond expected baselines. Common root causes include prompt injection attacks that balloon context windows, misconfigured retrieval pipelines appending oversized document chunks, or viral traffic patterns triggering unbounded parallelism.

Latency incidents are often correlated: large prompts not only cost more but also saturate model inference queues, pushing p95 and p99 response times into unacceptable ranges. Effective triage requires correlating token-usage metrics with request traces.

Engineers should track tokens-per-request distributions, cost-per-session, and time-to-first-token (TTFT) alongside total generation time. Alerting should fire on both absolute thresholds (e.g., daily spend > $X) and relative anomalies (e.g., average tokens up 3× from the rolling 1-hour baseline).

Rate limiting, prompt length caps, and circuit breakers are the primary containment tools once an incident is confirmed.

LLM providers — whether OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, or self-hosted endpoints — are subject to regional outages, rate-limit storms, and degraded-mode operations. A resilient LLM application must never depend on a single provider.

The canonical fallback architecture uses a priority-ordered provider list managed by an LLM gateway or proxy layer (e.g., LiteLLM, Portkey, or a custom router). When the primary provider returns HTTP 5xx errors, timeouts, or exceeds a configurable error-rate threshold within a rolling window, the gateway automatically promotes the next candidate.

Key engineering challenges include prompt compatibility (different providers tokenize and interpret system prompts differently), output schema consistency (JSON mode availability varies), and latency normalization across providers with different performance profiles. Fallback routing should be tested regularly using synthetic failure injection — temporarily blocking the primary endpoint — to validate that SLA commitments are met during failover.

Runbook procedures must document which models are considered semantically equivalent and what quality trade-offs are accepted during a degraded fallback state.

A postmortem transforms an incident from a failure into an organizational learning asset. The blameless postmortem principle — foundational in modern SRE culture — holds that individuals acted rationally given the information and tooling available; systemic improvements, not personal accountability, are the goal.

An LLMOps postmortem document should capture: a precise incident timeline, the detection mechanism and time-to-detect (TTD), the time-to-mitigate (TTM), the root cause analysis (using 5-Whys or fishbone diagrams), the customer and business impact, and a prioritized list of action items with owners and due dates. For LLM-specific incidents, the postmortem must also address model behavior factors: Did a prompt change introduce the regression?

Was a safety classifier threshold misconfigured? Did retrieval pipeline changes expand the attack surface?

Action items fall into three categories: detection improvements (add monitoring, lower alert thresholds), prevention improvements (add prompt validation, improve chunking logic), and response improvements (update runbooks, add killswitch automation). A reliability review cadence — typically monthly — tracks whether action items are closed and measures trend data on TTD, TTM, and incident frequency.

Over time, this creates a compounding improvement effect that measurably raises system reliability and safety.
